figures.takeaway: When a robot copies an expert, its small slips pile up: a task twice as long leaves it about four times as far off course.
The robot's next move blends three overlapping plans, and the oldest plan gets the biggest say.
Averaging an old plan with a late new one can send the robot on a move neither plan chose, straight into the obstacle.
Starting from random guesses and cleaning them up, the robot ends with two separate good moves instead of one blurred average.
Each moment of an arm's movement is written as seven words, one for each direction of motion, so a language model can produce it.
Several small refining steps land on the right move where one big jump misses, and each step costs time.
Through 2025 every robot model here said how it produces motion, but most 2026 entries do not disclose it.
A robot's plan changes slowly while its motor commands come fast: about 100 of them while the plan changes twice.
The robot's computer takes more than twice as long to choose a move as the arm can wait between commands.
A robot handed a new plan mid-motion can pause, lurch or blend the two plans.
Describing actions as where the hand moves, instead of joint angles, lets one model learn from many robots and from human videos.
Walling off the language part of the model while the robot learns to move protects what it knows about language and trains faster.
Walking legs cope with small errors in the simulated ground, but fitting a tight part leaves almost no room for error.
Running thousands of practice robots at once on one graphics chip cuts training from hours to minutes, but the speed-up levels off.
A robot that cannot see the ground can still learn its shape by feeling it through its legs.
Going from walking to hopping, a four-legged robot keeps fewer feet on the ground, trading steadiness for bounce.
Humanoid control is split into layers, slow decisions on top and fast balancing below.
The scoring rule decides how a learning robot walks: change what earns points and a different walk comes out.
World models differ in what they imagine: some predict full pictures of what comes next, others only a compact summary.
The further ahead a robot imagines, the more its imagined path drifts from what really happens.
The robot plans by trying moves in its compact mental summary and keeping whichever brings it closest to the goal.
Robot training data is tiny next to the text used to train chatbots: ten part-time robots would need 143 years to collect 10,000 hours.
Mixing the robot's own guess of where it is with a noisy sensor reading gives an estimate surer than either one alone.
Three fingertips placed well around a box hold it against a push from any direction.
The robot's next move blends three overlapping plans, and the oldest plan gets the biggest say.
When fingers block the camera's view, touch sensors in the fingertips can still feel the object slipping.
Experts hold six competing bets on how robots will become generally capable, and each bet names the result that would prove it wrong.
Planning 100 moves at a time instead of one at a time raised the simulated robot's success from 1% to 44%.
The robot plans 1.6 seconds ahead, carries out only the first half, then plans again.
Physical Intelligence released a new robot model every few months, and only the first three are confirmed downloadable.
Thirteen general-purpose robot models have come out since early 2025, and only four can be downloaded.
Practice that would take a real robot months takes a simulator minutes, because learning by trial and error needs millions of tries.
A robot trained on one floor does best there, while one trained on many varied floors copes with all of them.
An AI writes the scoring rules a robot learns from, reads how the robot did, and fixes rules that reward the wrong thing.
A robot that plans ahead fails when its guesses about the world are wrong, and one that learned by practice fails on surprises it never practised.
A useful video model predicts a different future when the robot's action changes.
Even when a picking robot succeeds 99% of the time, slow jam fixes can eat 19 minutes of every hour.
The longer each jam takes a person to fix, the longer a picking robot takes to pay for itself.
The robot's search grows random branches into open space until one reaches the goal, and that branch is the path around the obstacles.
To hold the pole upright the motor must push back harder than gravity pulls; push too gently and the pole sags over.
An arm that controls how hard it pushes can be set soft enough to touch a fragile object without crushing it; a stiff arm that only follows a position cannot.
A camera tilted a fraction of a degree off makes the robot miss, and the miss grows the farther away the object is.
The way a robot stores a scene decides which questions it can answer; finer resolution only changes cost and detail.
Small errors in every turn bend a robot's map out of shape; when it recognises a place it has been, the map is pulled back, with every step taking a little of the correction.
No outside auditor has checked any of these humanoid work records, so they are company claims, not proven performance.
None of these robot hands publishes both its touch sensitivity and its price.
Robots finished more tasks as they trained on more human video, but the study stopped at 20,000 hours, so anything beyond that is a guess.
Eight results would show robotics is not overhyped; as of August 2026 none has fully happened and four are partly there.
The faster a drone's camera reports an obstacle, the faster the drone can safely fly.
A slower camera forces the drone to fly slower to stay safe, cutting its top speed from about 69 to 53 km/h here.
Tagging each step as helping or hurting shows the robot that its failure was caused by a crooked grip 20 seconds earlier.
A realistic picture of a mug cannot be pushed, because it has no weight or friction until someone adds physics.
After one small slip, a robot trained by copying lands where it has no examples to follow, and its mistakes grow.
Even a robot that gets each step 95% right usually fails a long job, so every step has to be almost perfect.
The faster a robot moves, the bigger the gap it must keep from people.
After one small slip, a robot trained by copying lands where it has no examples to follow, and its mistakes grow.
After practice with EXPO-FT, the robot succeeded on all 30 tries on each of four tasks, ahead of the other methods.
At 95% success per step about half of 14-step jobs fail, because a long job works only if every step works.
Turning the shoulder swings the whole rest of the arm, hand included, along with it.
Even with noisy readings that sometimes drop out, the filter tracks the target, and it grows less sure while readings are missing.
A straight-line shortcut matches a curved motion only close to the robot's best guess; the less sure the robot is, the further the shortcut drifts from the truth.
A wrong measurement anywhere between the arm, the camera and the hand moves where the hand lands.
The AI never drives the motors itself: every move it suggests passes a safety check first.
The faster the arm moves, the further a late camera photo misplaces its hand.
Hand-eye calibration needs at least three poses, and after about a dozen more poses barely help.
A camera queue that keeps the last ten pictures makes the model act on pictures a third of a second old.
Nodes stream with topics, ask quick questions with services, and run long cancellable jobs with actions.
A robot that learns only from old records overrates actions it never tried, unless it is made cautious about them.
Learning from old runs can join the good parts of two runs into a success that neither run reached alone.
Adding reinforcement learning to robots trained on recorded data raised their real-world success in four studies.
A humanoid run by one whole-body model picks things up less reliably the lower they sit, worst from the floor.
A walking robot trained in a simulator with perfect motors falls on real legs; simulating the real motors lets it walk.
Training moves each simulated robot to harder ground when it copes and to easier ground when it struggles.
Copying a person's movements straight onto a robot with different proportions leaves its feet floating or sinking.
One graphics chip can simulate thousands of practising robots at once, far more than older computer simulators.
Newton keeps several physics solvers behind one interface and hands each kind of material to the one built for it.
An on-policy learner throws each batch of experience away after using it; an off-policy learner keeps every batch to learn from again.
A missed goal can still teach a robot once the push is relabelled with the spot it actually reached.
A scanned copy of a lab only predicted real robot results after its simulation settings were tuned.
A policy trained in simulation inherits its contact model's mistakes; one copied from real demonstrations needs no contact model.
Even the robot hand that solved a Rubik's cube in simulation finished the real scramble in only 2 of 10 tries.
To test a robot on places it has never seen, keep whole scenes out of training; a random split of episodes puts every test scene into training too.
A surgical robot divides the surgeon's hand movement before it reaches the instrument, so at 3 to 1 a 30 mm stroke, wobble and all, moves the tip only 10 mm.
In Figure's Helix 02 the whole-body controller acts five times for every joint target the layer above it sets: 1,000 times a second against 200.
The bear case rests on four premises, each broken by its own result, and it falls only when all four results are in; by August 2026 none was.
A safety filter leaves a learned policy's proposal alone wherever it is safe and, where it is not, changes it by the least amount that keeps the robot out, so the simple filter is what gets checked.
An excavator that learned a model of its own arm from its own moves tracked paths after 20 minutes as well as earlier controllers trained for 100 to 150.
A planner picks the action its learned model scores highest, so it lands past the data, where the model only extrapolates and its score is wrong.
An impedance action sends a target and a stiffness: past a surface the tool stops, and the push is the stiffness times how far the target sits past it.
Gemini Robotics answers in about 250 ms yet controls at 50 Hz because each answer carries a chunk of actions; 13 or more cover the wait, fewer leave the arm idle.
A point a model picks in an image fixes only a line from the camera; a depth reading picks the spot on that line the arm should reach.

A leader arm built as a smaller twin of the robot sends each joint's reading to the robot's same joint unchanged, so the robot copies the operator joint for joint and the demonstration is already in the robot's joint space.
At Level 1 the robot takes over one supervised task: with ScoPilot on, Maestro's arm keeps the laparoscope aimed at the instrument tip, while the surgeon still moves every instrument.

Steering a frozen policy's noise, as DSRL does, only ever lands on actions the policy already makes, so a skill it never learned stays out of reach; a small edit on the action, as in EXPO, can step past them.

An end-effector delta is only numbers until its frame is named: a move recorded in the tool's frame and replayed in the table's frame lands somewhere else once the tool is turned, and agrees only when the tool is square.

A person's joint angles copied onto a robot of other proportions put its hand on a skewed path, while the hand's own motion, replayed from wherever the robot's hand is, draws the same stroke, which is why human and robot data can share relative end-effector actions.
Counting recorded runs and counting hours rank robot datasets differently: AgiBot World has about 25 times FineART's runs but under twice its hours, because FineART's runs are much longer.
Robot arms on sale cost from about $300 to $70,000 and humanoids from about $5,000 to $30,000, while several humanoid makers publish no price at all.
Recording demonstrations with a handheld gripper was three times faster than steering a robot, though about half as fast as doing the task by hand.
